node.label: E. A. Wrigley
node.date_label: Cambridge Group founded (with Laslett) 1964 · with Schofield, The Population History of England 1981 · Ellen McArthur lectures 1987 · Continuity, Chance and Change 1988 · with Davies, Oeppen and Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1997 · Poverty, Progress, and Population 2004 · Energy and the English Industrial Revolution 2010 · The Path to Sustained Growth 2016
node.description: A historical demographer and economic historian at Cambridge, who founded the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure with Peter Laslett in 1964. With Roger Schofield he reconstructed England’s population from the registers of 404 parishes by “back projection”, making it “possible for the first time” to follow “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981); a family-reconstitution study, a technique perfected by Louis Henry, was its complement (1997). He called the industrial revolution his “first main research interest”, to which he “returned increasingly” after years of population history. In Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), from his 1987 Ellen McArthur lectures, he questioned it as “a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon”: growth came from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time”, as an “organic economy” bounded by the productivity of the land met a new one using mineral energy. Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010) asked “not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end”, without offering energy as the only explanation: there could be “no single, ‘true’ account”, and to downplay institutional and scientific explanations would be “presumptuous and mildly ridiculous”. Mining coal “provided the solution” (2016). He judged Rostow’s “take-off” “now almost impossible to maintain” (2004). Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990). Readers set his energy argument beside Pomeranz’s coal (Mokyr in a draft of 2002, Huang in 2002, Clark and Jacks in 2007), and Wong said that China Transformed had followed his arguments on coal (2016).
node.representative_figures_and_works: E. A. (Tony) Wrigley (1931–2022); with R. S. Schofield, The Population History of England, 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981); People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change: The Character of the Industrial Revolution in England (1988); with R. S. Davies, J. E. Oeppen and R. S. Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution, 1580–1837 (1997); Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004); Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010); “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 2013); The Path to Sustained Growth (2016). Co-founder, with Peter Laslett, of the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964). Readers and critics: Maxine Berg and Pat Hudson (1990); Joel Mokyr and Philip Huang (2002); Gregory Clark and David Jacks (2007); R. Bin Wong (2016).
node.scope_note: Read in Cambridge University Press excerpts: The Population History of England (1981; the introduction of the 1989 paperback, pp. 1–5, OCRed), English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997, pp. 3–4), Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11), on 2026-10-18; Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, pp. 1–4) in revision 1.145; the 2013 article in abstract only. The Cambridge Group’s founding and projects come from its institutional history. The rest of each book is unread, including the statistical reconstruction, and no estimate is adjudicated; Berg and Hudson’s objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate studies, not the reconstruction as such; the reconstruction and the reconstitution volume were collaborative, with Schofield, Oeppen and Davies. People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread. The comparisons with Pomeranz are readers’: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read. Wong’s statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is his 2016 retrospective. The wider argument about why industrialisation happened in Britain is held by the debate entry capitalismdebates; his population work stays on demography/aggregate_population.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reconstructing England’s population from parish registers: with Schofield, 404 parishes and “back projection” to trace “a secular cycle of population development” and its relation to economic change (1981), complemented by family reconstitution (1997), in the Cambridge Group he co-founded (1964)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981; introduction pp. 1–5 read in the publisher excerpt of the 1989 Cambridge paperback, OCRed): “since pre-industrial societies normally experienced great difficulty in achieving a rapid expansion in their capacity to produce goods and services, population was the more dynamic element in the striking of a balance with production” (p. 1); the registers make it “possible for the first time to establish with some precision what changes took place in a pre-industrial population over a period of time long enough to encompass a secular cycle of population development, and to investigate the relationship between demographic and economic change during its course” (p. 2); monthly totals “taken from the registers of a total of 404 parishes” (p. 3); “the technique of back projection, which was developed to make the best use of the aggregative data assembled” (p. 4); the aggregative tabulations began as “a subsidiary element” of the Cambridge Group’s family-reconstitution work of “the middle 1960s” (p. 5). Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997, pp. 3–4, read): “This book is intended as a complement to the Population history of England”; family reconstitution “had then recently been perfected by Louis Henry”. The Cambridge Group’s institutional history (read) dates its founding by Laslett and Wrigley to 1964. A collaborative project: Schofield, Oeppen and Davies share these results, and the reconstruction’s estimates are not adjudicated here. Berg and Hudson’s critique of its “aggregative” use for causal analysis is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

proposed_edges.relationship: Technologies to exploit coal as Europe’s difference: China Transformed (1997) followed “arguments of E. A. Wrigley”, as Wong recalled in 2016
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, p. 76, read): “The cluster of differences stressed in that work concerned European science and technologies, and in particular, following arguments of E. A. Wrigley, the importance of technologies to exploit coal as a source of energy to power new kinds of machines”; his note cites Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Qualification: this is Wong’s retrospective account. China Transformed is read only in chapter openings, and the passage that cites Wrigley there was not read. Wrigley’s own organic-economy argument is on e_a_wrigley → capitalismdebates (edge_1084).

proposed_edges.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.
